common_name: Butterfly Japanese Maple (Small Variegated Blue-Green Upright Maple)

planting.note: Plant in spring or fall in a sheltered site with rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun; Butterfly bears small, variegated blue-green leaves edged in white and pink on a slender, upright small tree.

directions: Plant in partial shade to morning sun in rich, moist, well-drained soil, sheltered from the hottest afternoon exposure that can scorch the variegated leaves. Butterfly bears small, deeply lobed blue-green leaves irregularly margined in white and flushed pink in spring, opening on a slender, upright, narrow small tree that fits tight spaces where a broad Japanese maple would be too large. Its variegated foliage brightens a shaded planting and provides multi-season color from spring through the fall display of pink-and-orange tones. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, and prune only minimally in late winter to shape and remove crossing branches.

common_name: Mikawa Yatsubusa Japanese Maple (Dwarf Dense Layered Bonsai-Type Maple)

planting.note: Plant in spring or fall in a sheltered site with rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun, or grow in a container; Mikawa Yatsubusa is a dwarf, densely layered maple popular for bonsai and small-garden use.

directions: Plant in partial shade to morning sun in rich, moist, well-drained soil, or grow in a container where its dwarf, densely branched habit is easy to display up close. Mikawa Yatsubusa forms a slow-growing, tightly congested mound of overlapping, layered green foliage with unusually short internodes, giving it a dense, textural look prized both as a landscape dwarf specimen and as classic bonsai stock. Its very slow growth rate and compact ultimate size make it one of the most practical Japanese maples for small gardens or container culture. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, and prune only minimally in late winter to shape.

common_name: Beni Otake Japanese Maple (Narrow Bamboo-Leaf Red Maple)

planting.note: Plant in spring or fall in a sheltered site with rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun; Beni Otake bears narrow, bamboo-like red leaves that hold their color through summer better than many red maple cultivars.

directions: Plant in partial shade to morning sun in rich, moist, well-drained soil, sheltered from the hottest afternoon exposure. Beni Otake, an unusual linearilobum-type cultivar, bears narrow, elongated, bamboo-like leaves in a rich red that holds its color through summer heat notably better than many other red-leaved Japanese maple cultivars, giving it a fine, distinctive texture unlike the broader lobed leaves of most maples. Its upright, vigorous habit and long-lasting color make it a strong specimen for a shaded or partly sunny border. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, and prune only minimally in late winter to shape and remove crossing branches.

common_name: Viridis Japanese Maple (Classic Green Mounding Lace-Leaf Maple)

planting.note: Plant in spring or fall in a sheltered site with rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun; Viridis is a classic mounding green lace-leaf maple with fine-textured foliage and gold-orange fall color.

directions: Plant in partial shade to morning sun in rich, moist, well-drained soil, sheltered from the hottest afternoon exposure. Viridis forms a graceful, low, mounding dome of finely dissected, lacy green foliage, the classic green counterpart to the many red-leaved lace-leaf cultivars, turning brilliant gold and orange in fall for a dramatic seasonal transformation. Its wider-than-tall, cascading habit makes it a strong specimen for the edge of a pond, atop a slope, or spilling over a low wall. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, especially through the first few years, and prune only minimally in late winter to remove crossing or dead branches, preserving the natural mounding form.

common_name: Osakazuki Japanese Maple (Green Summer Foliage with Brilliant Scarlet Fall Color)

planting.note: Plant in spring or fall in a sheltered site with rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun; Osakazuki is grown chiefly for its exceptionally brilliant scarlet fall color, considered among the best of any Japanese maple.

directions: Plant in partial shade to morning sun in rich, moist, well-drained soil, sheltered from the hottest afternoon exposure. Osakazuki bears plain green summer foliage on a larger, upright tree, unremarkable through most of the growing season, but transforms each fall into one of the most brilliant, saturated scarlet-red displays of any commonly grown Japanese maple, a dramatic payoff that has made it a longtime favorite among collectors specifically for autumn color. Its larger mature size suits it to a specimen role in a spacious garden where its fall show can be viewed from a distance. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, and prune only minimally in late winter to shape and remove crossing branches.

common_name: Ukigumo Japanese Maple (Floating Clouds Heavily Variegated Maple)

planting.note: Plant in spring or fall in a sheltered site with rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun; Ukigumo, meaning 'floating clouds,' bears heavily variegated white, pink, and green mottled leaves.

directions: Plant in partial shade to morning sun in rich, moist, well-drained soil, sheltered from the hottest afternoon exposure that can scorch the delicate variegated leaves. Ukigumo, Japanese for 'floating clouds,' bears leaves heavily mottled and speckled in white, pink, and green in an irregular, ever-shifting pattern that makes each leaf slightly different, one of the most dramatically variegated Japanese maple cultivars available, on a slow-growing, upright small tree. Its striking, ethereal foliage pattern makes a strong focal specimen in a shaded or partly sunny border where its color can be appreciated up close. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, and prune only minimally in late winter to shape.

common_name: Villa Taranto Japanese Maple (Narrow Strap-Leaf Compact Dome Maple)

planting.note: Plant in spring or fall in a sheltered site with rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun; Villa Taranto is a linearilobum-type maple with narrow, strap-like reddish-green lobes on a compact, dome-shaped bush.

directions: Plant in partial shade to morning sun in rich, moist, well-drained soil, sheltered from the hottest afternoon exposure. Villa Taranto, a linearilobum-type Japanese maple, bears unusually narrow, strap-like leaf lobes in reddish-green that give the foliage a fine, feathery, almost willow-like texture distinct from the broader lobed leaves of typical maple cultivars, on a compact, dome-shaped shrub. Its fine texture and manageable size make it a good specimen for a small garden or container where a delicate, airy foliage effect is wanted. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, and prune only minimally in late winter to shape.

common_name: Beni-kawa Japanese Maple (Coral Bark Maple with Salmon-Red Winter Stems)

planting.note: Plant in spring or fall in a sheltered site with rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun; Beni-kawa is a coral bark maple with softer salmon-red winter stems, slightly smaller than the popular Sango-kaku.

directions: Plant in partial shade to morning sun in rich, moist, well-drained soil, sheltered from the hottest afternoon exposure. Beni-kawa is a coral bark maple selected for winter stem color, its young branches turning a soft salmon-pink to coral-red as cold weather sets in, a slightly gentler, more muted tone than the vivid coral of the popular Sango-kaku on a somewhat smaller-growing tree. Green summer foliage turns gold in fall before dropping to reveal the colorful winter bark display, giving this cultivar strong multi-season interest. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, and prune only minimally in late winter, since young, brightly colored stems provide the best winter color.

common_name: Inaba Shidare Japanese Maple (Vigorous Upright-Growing Red Weeping Maple)

planting.note: Plant in spring or fall in a sheltered site with rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun; Inaba Shidare is a more vigorous, upright-growing weeping lace-leaf maple with rich red foliage that holds color well.

directions: Plant in partial shade to morning sun in rich, moist, well-drained soil, sheltered from the hottest afternoon exposure. Inaba Shidare grows more vigorously and taller than many other weeping lace-leaf maples before its branches begin cascading, ultimately reaching greater height while still forming the graceful mounding, umbrella-like silhouette typical of the dissectum group, its deeply cut leaves holding a rich, saturated red color through summer better than many red lace-leaf cultivars. Its combination of vigor and reliable color has made it one of the most widely planted red weeping maples. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, especially through the first few years, and prune only minimally in late winter to remove crossing or dead branches.

common_name: Cathedral Live Oak (Pyramidal Strong-Leader Live Oak Selection)

planting.note: Plant container trees in fall or early spring in well-drained to moist, deep soil in full sun; Cathedral is a live oak selection bred for a strong central leader and pyramidal-to-ovoid form, a better street and urban tree shape than the wide-spreading straight species.

directions: Plant in well-drained to moist, deep soil in full sun; live oak tolerates a wide range of soils including compacted urban sites once established. Cathedral was selected specifically for a strong central leader and a more pyramidal-to-ovoid canopy shape than the enormous, wide-spreading form typical of straight-species Southern live oak, making it far better suited to street plantings, medians, and smaller urban and suburban lots where the species' eventual 60-100 foot spread would be impractical. It retains the same tough, evergreen, wind- and salt-tolerant character that makes live oak the iconic Gulf Coast landscape tree. Water deeply during establishment, and prune minimally to develop good branch structure while the tree is young.

common_name: Highrise Live Oak (Narrow Columnar Live Oak for Tight Urban Sites)

planting.note: Plant container trees in fall or early spring in well-drained to moist, deep soil in full sun; Highrise is a narrow, upright live oak selection reaching only about 25 feet wide versus 60-100 feet for the species, developed for tight urban sites.

directions: Plant in well-drained to moist, deep soil in full sun; live oak tolerates a wide range of soils including compacted urban sites once established. Highrise, patented as QVTIA, was bred specifically for an unusually narrow, upright canopy, spreading only about twenty-five feet wide compared to the sixty to one hundred foot spread of the straight species, making it one of the only live oak selections practical for street tree plantings, narrow medians, and other tight urban sites where a full-sized live oak canopy would conflict with buildings or utilities. It retains the same tough, evergreen, wind- and salt-tolerant character that makes live oak the iconic Gulf Coast landscape tree. Water deeply during establishment, and prune minimally to develop good branch structure while the tree is young.

common_name: Highpoint Nuttall Oak (Fast-Growing Own-Root Nuttall Oak Selection)

planting.note: Plant container trees in fall or early spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Highpoint is a fast-growing, own-root Nuttall oak selection with a uniform oval crown and bronze-red new growth, tolerant of wet, clay bottomland soils.

directions: Plant in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral, deep soil in full sun; Nuttall oak tolerates seasonal flooding and heavy clay far better than most oaks, making it a strong choice for bottomland and low-lying sites. Highpoint, patented as QNFTA, is a clonally propagated, own-root Nuttall oak selection valued for uniform, symmetrical oval crown development and attractive bronze-red new growth in spring, offering more predictable landscape performance than seedling-grown trees of variable form. It shares the species' brilliant red fall color, one of the best displays among Southern bottomland oaks. Water deeply during establishment, and prune minimally to develop good branch structure while the tree is young.

common_name: Hightower Willow Oak (Uniform Pyramidal Clonal Willow Oak Selection)

planting.note: Plant container trees in fall or early spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Hightower was the first clonally propagated willow oak cultivar, selected for a strong central leader and uniform pyramidal form.

directions: Plant in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral, deep soil in full sun. Hightower, patented as QPSTA, was the first willow oak selection propagated clonally rather than from seed, chosen for a strong central leader and consistently uniform, pyramidal-to-oval canopy that gives far more predictable street and shade tree performance than the variable form typical of seedling-grown willow oaks. It shares the species' fine, narrow, willow-like leaves, fast growth rate, and adaptability to a range of soils that have made willow oak a widely planted Southern shade and street tree. Water deeply during establishment, and prune minimally to develop good branch structure while the tree is young.
